subtitle: Hunting Global Value - Japanese Healthcare, European Logistics, and a Capital-Light Net-Net - Here's What I've Been Buying
title: April 2026 Portfolio Review
description: Hunting Global Value - Japanese Healthcare, European Logistics, and a Capital Light Net-Net - Here's What I've Been Buying
body_html:
Disclaimer: By reading this article, you acknowledge and agree to the terms and conditions

What is it worth to you?

That’s a question I think of often when it comes to AI. In both markets and in real life, everything is relative. You buy a stock when you think it’s worth more than what it’s trading for, you buy a preferred when the risk adjusted yield in excess of what you might earn in cash, you buy a product when the value it provides to you exceeds the price; the larger the differential, the happier you are to do it, and the more you want of it.

Over the past couple of weeks, we’ve seen countless complaints on Twitter and tech news from angry customers asserting Claude has “dumbed down” its models or ChatGPT was throttling usage. While many were quick to jump on the companies and assert they were doing this because the business model was unprofitable, I see it differently: the complaining highlights how large the value differential is.

A junior software developer (at least in the US) might cost $75,000 - $150,000, and I think most would agree Codex or Claude Code is akin to having a developer on call 24/7. AI serves as a personal butler when it comes to researching, finding restaurants, maybe even locating cheap laptop deals. It’s not perfect, but things are moving quickly. With that in mind, the price of a $100 Claude Max or ChatGPT Pro plan is actually a bargain to power users. When a $100 plan gets throttled, users riot because they are losing way more than $100 in value.

Even if the labs hiked pricing to $500 or $1,000 a month, it would still be a bargain to the power users driving AI demand. The price of a token to a company using AI to handle things like phone support or data entry is still significantly underpriced.

This isn’t a mere anecdotal observation, the proof is in insatiable demand. Anthropic’s ARR has surged to $30 Billion from $9 Billion in just 3 and a half months. Nebius (a leading neocloud) is sold out of capacity. Rental Rates for older H100 Chips are up significantly, and in fact have risen since 2024. It doesn’t seem like things are slowing down at all.

My point is, the value AI brings to the table far exceeds the cost, and with that in mind it’s easy to see why the Hyperscalers and Frontier AI Labs alike are clamoring for more chips: the value of the chips, to them, significantly exceeds the price, and the value of the “tokens” they provide to their clients also significantly exceeds the cost. As long as that is the case, I think the AI trade has legs, and that AI adoption will continue accelerating.

The AI Megabasket I posted earlier this year has been a major driver of returns in my portfolio. I’ve made a few adjustments, and have cut several of the more speculative names. My Memory and Storage portfolio is just SK Hynix, Samsung, Western Digital, Micron, and Kioxia (in that order), and my Infrastructure basket is comprised of IES Holdings, Comfort Systems, and Powell Industries.

Has my portfolio been fully “AI Pilled”? A bit, but I also see a lot of value in inexpensive banking, insurance, and discount-to-nav situations with aligned management teams and aggressive capital allocation plans to address the discount.

The “Blackjack 21” index continues to set All Time Highs and is up 16.4% YTD on an equal-weight basis. While it might not seem like much next to the AI names, it is significantly ahead of the MSCI Global Financials Index (-0.83%), the S&P 500 Financials Index (-5.20%). I think components in this basket still have significant tailwinds: Japanese banks are poised to gain from rising yields, and the aggressive capital allocation of Halyk Savings Bank, NT Butterfield, Georgia Capital, and International General Insurance continue to drive returns and improve ROE.

Before I get into the list of all 45 Portfolio holdings, I wanted to discuss the significant opportunity Global Value presents. The MSCI EAFE and MSCI Emerging Indexes are finally putting on a show after more than a decade of significant underperformance relative to US Equities.

While some of the reversion is due to Korean Equities (which is almost purely an AI trade), I think there is a long-term tailwind from improving global capital allocation and the “Americanization” of foreign equities. Japan, Korea, China, and the EU are putting increasing amounts of focus on corporate capital allocation. Japanese companies who used to rewards shareholders with “Yutai” (gifts such as discount cards and food) have pivoted to share repurchases, and management teams have aspirational Price to Book Ratios, European companies (who were previously allergic to anything other than a mediocre dividend) are wading their way into buybacks. The bottom line is these companies are finally being run for the benefit of the shareholders.

While the broader indexes have surged as a result, however, many small cap names with improving fundamentals and shareholder friendly capital allocation have been entirely left behind due to their lower liquidity and limited Institutional interest.

I think these setups are exactly where retail investors have an edge: finding companies with strong capital allocation, aligned management teams, and inflecting fundamentals that are simply too small for larger investors to touch. If you think about it, the liquidity discount does make sense. If you are a large Institutional Investor looking at two identical companies at the same valuation, but one has $1 Million in ADV while the other has $10 Million in ADV, you’ll of course opt for the more liquid investment. Over time, however, I think you can generate significantly higher returns by exploiting this phenomenon and positioning yourself in names at a valuation discount that have aggressive capital allocation plans in place to close the gap.

I haven’t pitched Japanese Equities since last summer. All four Japanese picks have significantly outperformed the broader index as well as the S&P, and astoundingly, three out of four have further 30-60% upside to Tangible Book Value.

After spending a lot of time screening, I’ve found two new Japanese companies with a similar setup, as well as three other value names that I believe are wrongly discounted. Before we get into the existing portfolio, here are the new positions.

Trade 1: “Buy a Pile of Cash, Get a Business, Free”

Long MOMO US Equity

Sector: Technology

Conviction: Medium

Current Price: $6.29

End of Year Target: $7.00

Forward P/E: 6.5x

Price / Tangible Book Value: 0.66x

Price / Adjusted Tangible Book Value: 0.90x

Shareholder Return Yield: 16.4% (Dividend: 4.7%, Share Repurchases: 11.7%)

Hello Group (MOMO US) is a Chinese social media company operating two flagship apps: Momo, a social networking and live streaming platform, and Tantan, a dating app commonly considered to be the Chinese version of Tinder. Momo’s domestic Chinese business has been in a steady decline, paying users have plummeted from a peak of 9 Million to just 3.5 Million driven by competition from Douyin (Chinese TikTok) and a years long crackdown on underreporting of tipping and gift income earned by livestreamers.

Momo stock is down nearly 90% from its 2017 Peak of $50 and seemingly prices in imminent implosion, but I think there is more to the story here. Momo’s Q4 2025 report just a few weeks ago showed the situation is inflecting: Chinese paying users have stabilized after an all time low of 3.5 Million in Q2 and climbed sequentially to 3.7 Million in Q3 and 3.9 Million in Q4, the first two consecutive quarters of growth since 2021. Additionally “overseas revenue” from Momo’s global portfolio (Happn – European Dating App, Soulchill – MENA Live Streaming Platform) has been accelerating. The International Portfolio of apps, which just a few years ago comprised just 1.6% of Revenue ($230 M RMB), now comprises 19.3% of Revenue ($2 B RMB) and have been guided as within striking distance of $3 B RMB in 2026:

“Something like RMB 3 billion in overseas revenue for 2026 is a pretty achievable target.” – Peng Hui – CFO, Q4 2025 Earnings Call

MOMO has always been viewed with wariness by American investors due to its VIE (Variable Interest Entity) structure, common among Chinese ADRs. MOMO itself does not own its Chinese operations, it instead has contractual economic rights to receive dividends from its Chinese business. Due to the VIE structure, significant cash (1.5 Billion RMB) is required to remain on the Mainland as “a statutory reserve”, and any dividends remitted to the overseas entity is assessed an additional 10% withholding tax on top of Corporate Income Taxes. While this setup isn’t optimal, Momo has routinely demonstrated excellent capital management and a willingness to move cash out of the Mainland to reward shareholders. Over the past 5 years, Momo has moved 11.4 Billion RMB (approximately $1.58 Billion USD) for use in share repurchases and dividends.

Much of the 2024 distribution was used to pay back bank loans at the parent level as well as a Tax Settlement for prior year taxes. Nevertheless, MOMO’s history of paying dividends to its parent entity is demonstrative that the cash profits generated in China are not trapped.

Additionally, since 2021 MOMO has been using cash paid offshore to reward the shareholders. In fact, MOMO has paid out more than 100% of adjusted net income in the form of repurchases and dividends 3 out of the last 5 years.

I think the capital return intensity is what differentiates MOMO from typical value traps. Anyone with a screener can find names at < 7x earnings, but how many of the names that show up return 100% of income, or even 50%, to the shareholders? Very few.

MOMO’s core business is capital light, and the balance sheet is comprised entirely of cold, hard cash. Essentially, MOMO shares are a pile of cash with a gushing app business on the side.

MOMO isn’t risk free, a sudden Chinese crackdown on VIE’s could ravage the company (as well as other VIE’s such as BABA, NIO, etc), although it is important to note MOMO’s Cayman Shell isn’t totally empty, the European and Japanese app portfolio is not subject to Chinese regulation. There is also the prospect of a continued Chinese crackdown on livestreaming and dating apps, which would significantly harm Momo and Tantan.

While this obvious downside exists, I also think there is significant upwards optionality. MOMO’s portfolio of International apps is rapidly growing, and much of the portfolio is not yet monetized which will provide a further tailwind once it is:

“We expect Yaahlan to turn profitable within this year, and Amar should be behind it by half a year or so. The AI-driven product in MiraiMind remains in investment mode as we prioritize user growth and product capability. We don’t want to focus too much on reaching profitability -- the ability for that product. But of course, for each of the region we are in, we also have a payback period that’s required.” – 2025 Q4 Earnings Call

MOMO currently trades at $6.29, a steep discount to its $7.50 net cash balance. Even if you strip out the $1.5 Billion RMB in “statutory reserves” MOMO is required to keep onshore (which I think you should since that cash earns interest but is otherwise locked up), MOMO still has a net cash position of $6.13 per share.

MOMO insiders, including CEO Yan Tang, own 30% of the company (currently worth $300 Million) and are highly incentivized to do the right thing given executive compensation of $6.3 Million USD is just a fraction of their ownership stake. Insider selling from RSU’s has averaged < $10 Million a year, a minimal amount relative to both ownership and the company’s sizeable repurchases.

Simply put, at $6.29 a share, you are getting $6.13 in cash a share, along with an International portfolio of cash cow apps run by aligned insiders at a 100% payout ratio, for just a few cents. It doesn’t get more deep value than that.

MOMO has historically been very active in repurchasing shares in the $6 - $7 a share range (they repurchased 16.8 Million shares in 2025 at $6.84 a share), and I think they are likely to be even more aggressive in the $5 - $6 range, which creates a compelling setup if you are looking for a short-term trade. Of course, Dating Apps and AI Companions will never be seen as a “premium” or “quality” business, so I am not expecting it to trade at 10x or 15x earnings, but even a small re-rate to 8x earnings would imply $7.71 a share, significant upside from the current price and still just 1.25x MOMO’s cash pile (and below Tangible Book Value of $9.75). With all things China, it makes sense to approach your sizing conservatively (< 2.5%), but at the current valuation I believe the market is ascribing MOMO’s app portfolio zero value, and that it is worth considering a starter position at these prices.

Trade 2: “Japanese Healthcare at 6x Earnings”

Long 9220 JT Equity (FB Care Services)

Sector: Healthcare

Conviction: Medium

Price: 1224 Yen

End of Year Target: 1400 Yen

Forward P/E: 6x

Price / Tangible Book: 0.79x

Insider Ownership: 53%

Shareholder Return Yield: 6.5% (Dividend: 3.0%, Share Repurchases 3.5%)

FB Care Services is a Japanese microcap poised to ride the ever-increasing tailwind of Japan’s aging population. FB Care Services is an elderly care operator running two integrated business lines: welfare equipment (wheelchairs, in home hospital beds, walkers, 42% of revenue) and nursing and dementia care facilities (group homes, home healthcare visits, 58% of revenue). The two segments complement each other, the welfare equipment segment is used as a patient funnel to its nursing facilities division once customers require elevated levels of care, and approximately 80% of all services are covered and reimbursed by Japan’s Long-Term Care Insurance System (Japanese equivalent of Medicare). Whether you like it or not, the company is simply riding the wave of ever-increasing Japanese entitlement spending.

FB Care Services IPO’d in 2021 and opened at 1,800 Yen (a relatively steep valuation at the time) and quickly fell into the 800-900 Yen range. Despite the relatively stagnant stock price, FB continued to make significant progress, acquiring two care facilities in the Tokyo region, opening three additional facilities in Tokyo’s suburbs, and acquiring a healthcare furniture business in 2025. The M&A has been highly accretive, EPS has jumped from 166 Yen in 2023 to 183 Yen in 2025 and revenue continues to grow at a 5% CAGR.

The company is tightly held by the founding Yanagisawa Family (53% ownership) but has exhibited surprising shareholder friendly capital allocation. The company has steadily increased the dividend from an inaugural 25 Yen in 2023 to 38 Yen in 2025, and also conducted sizeable share repurchases in 2025, reducing shares outstanding by 8% (and the float by 16%).

The regular tenor of supportive share repurchases and dividend hikes have narrowed the discount to Tangible Book Value of 1510 Yen, but the stock still trades at a massive discount to closely comparable peers. FB Care trades at 6x earnings and 0.77x Tangible Book in comparison to Charm Care (6062) at 13x earnings, Care21 (2373) at 11x earnings, Saint-Care (2374) 17x earnings, and Solasto (6197) 11x earnings. I’m not saying FB should trade in the middle of the peer group (12x earnings), but even a small re-rate to 8x or 9x provides 50% upside, and I think the entire sector will continue to perform well as Japan’s population continues to age.

FB isn’t riskless, limited liquidity makes the name “off limits” to most Institutions other than the DSBI Japan Small Cap Absolute Value Fund, and Japan’s Long Term Care program is set to adjust regulatory nursing home rates in 2027. If rate adjustments don’t keep up with rising staffing costs, margins will fall.

Nonetheless, with shareholder friendly capital allocation, a massive structural tailwind driven by Japan’s aging population, and steadily growing fundamentals, I think FB Care at 6x earnings is too cheap to ignore. I have several outstanding orders in the 1100 – 1200 range, and when blocks occasionally come online, I add to my position. It’s a name I want to keep buying.

I know it is difficult to buy when the company itself is acquiring 16% of the float each year (at least in 2025), but I think that level of structural support provides a compelling setup in terms of price action, and that the share repurchases are highly accretive. I think one day FB Care will trade at or above Tangible Book Value of 1,510, and until then, I am happy to add slowly in the 1200s. If you have an interest in deep-value Japanese Small Caps, I think FB Care is worth adding to your watch list.

Trade 3: “Capital Light in Japan”

Long 7089 JT Equity (For Startups)

Sector: Recruitment Services

Conviction: Low

Price: 1224 Yen

End of Year Target: 1500 Yen

Forward P/E: 12x

Price to Tangible Book Value: 3.05x

Insider Ownership: 15%

Shareholder Return Yield: 2% (Share Repurchases Only)

For Startups is probably the most Japanese-esque company you can imagine, a Venture Fund, a Startup Database (of startups), and a Headhunter, all in one. What it truly represents, however, is a pure play way to ride the wave of exploding Japanese VC Activity in a capital-light vehicle.

For Startups is heavily ingrained in the Japanese start-up economy. It operates Startup DB, (Japan’s largest Startup Database – 10% of revenue) and uses it as a funnel for its VC-oriented headhunting division (Human Capital Division – 90% of revenue).

The company’s Human Capital Division is a success-fee-based headhunting division that caters exclusively to startups. For Startups charges clients 30 - 35% of a placed candidate’s first-year salary, and with Japan’s startup executive salaries running 6 – 12 Million Yen and the company increasingly focusing on C-Suite candidates, the average placement fee has soared 58% from 2.46 Million Yen in the 2020 IPO to 3.9 Million Yen in 2025. For Startup’s niche in Startup HR Services is highly defendable; its proprietary Startup DB Database allows it to rapidly identify Startups with significant hiring needs, and its connections to VC’s (who are also shareholders) such as Fukuoka Jisho, M3, Incubate Fund KK, Globis Capital Partners, Wil LLC, Strike CO, and Sparx Group have created a massive referral base: when these VC’s have portfolio companies that need to hire, they call up For Startups. The company also has a small co-invest platform in which it invests alongside its VC clients, the portfolio currently stands at 600 Million Yen (a little less than 10% of the market cap), and isn’t a meaningful financial position.

Earnings have soared from 22 Yen in 2021 to 99 Yen in 2025, and in February the company reported record guidance and pulled forward its 2027 forecast.

What piqued my interest is that the company stated it believes the “current share price level has not factored in growth potential of our business; we regard it as extremely undervalued”, and that it repurchased 160,000 shares (4% of the float) in March, showing that this statement wasn’t mere lip service.

With a 5-year revenue CAGR of 32% and a 5-year EPS CAGR of 79%, For Startups has clearly exhibited positive operating leverage and is poised to ride the wave of further VC and Private Equity investment in Japan.

Despite the record earnings, shareholder friendly capital allocation, and an extremely capital-light model, For Startups trades at a sizeable discount to closely comparable peers. Bizreach (4194) trades at 16x, JAC at 14x, En Japan at 16x, and Wantedly at 10x, For Startups, at just 12x. The discount is especially confounding given For Startup’s niche, it’s Startup DB Division (which likely demands a higher valuation), and that it grows at double the pace of peers.

Once again, I think the only realistic reason for the discount is lower liquidity. For Startups is a $50 Million USD market cap company, and a significant chunk of shares are held by insiders and affiliated VCs.

I think For Startups has all the markings of a fabled “capital light compounder”, aside from a migraine inducing multiple and the usual circle of GARP lovers who only seem to swoon for 6% growth at 35x earnings. At what is likely 11x forward earnings and with a differentiated business model and secular growth tailwind behind it, I think For Startups is too cheap to ignore. I have been adding shares in the 1200 Yen range, and ultimately I think For Startups should demand a premium to peers, perhaps 15x earnings which would imply upwards of 1,530 Yen a share.

Given the limited liquidity in the stock and the niche nature of the company, I don’t think this is a name you can size too largely, but similar to FB Care Services, I think small positions in both names provide an opportunity to add torque to your portfolio via Deep Value Japan Equities at palatable valuations with excellent capital allocation.

Trade 4: “Pawn Me”

Long CCV AU (Cash Converters)

Sector: Consumers

Conviction: High

Price: 0.295 AUD

End of Year Target Price: 0.40 AUD

Forward P/E: 8x

Price to Tangible Book Value: 1.05x

Insider Ownership: 40%

Shareholder Return Yield: 6% (Dividend Only)

I’ll try to keep this pitch brief since I covered Cash Converters in my Dividends, Discounts, Diamonds in the Rough piece from August 2025. Since then, the stock is down roughly 7%, but my conviction to the name has only increased as the company executes its plan.

Cash Converters International is an Australian consumer lender and pawnbroker operating 650 stores across Australia, New Zealand, Europe, and the UK.

Cash Converters is a comeback name. After decades of rapid global growth (via a franchise model) and an expansion into highly variable payday loans and vehicle finance that made the company “toxic” to investors and bank lenders alike, Cash Converters was on the brink of a twenty year low in 2020 as COVID struck and credit quality floundered.

The company’s CEO resigned and was replaced by Sam Budiselik, a member of the board with Investment Banking experience at Barclays, UBS, and Deutsch Bank. He embarked on three key initiatives: reducing corporate overhead, winding down Cash Converter’s toxic auto and payday lending segments, and using internally generated capital to acquire Australian and UK franchisees (many of whom were willing to sell their stores at just 3-5x EBITDA).

From 2020 to Q2 2025, Cash Converters acquired 79 franchises at an average price of $700k at under 5x EBITDA a location. The company generated a 15% IRR on these acquisitions, and the stores now contribute $6 M in after-tax profit. In late 2025, the company conducted a $25 Million Equity Raise at $0.305 a share to finance a large acquisition of 29 Australian Stores at $37 Million (4.5x EBITDA). The offering was structured as an acquisition rights distribution to existing shareholders.

Cash Converter’s has significantly restructured its loan book, which reduces earnings volatility, frees up capital, and removes the toxic overhang of the balance sheet. Payday Loans have declined from $82 Million in 2022 to just $22 Million in 2025 and are on track to hit zero in 2026. Similarly, high risk auto loans have declined from $70 Million in 2023 to $35 Million in 2025, and are set to fully run off by 2027. Cash Converter’s has been using the extra capital towards franchise acquisitions, and is rapidly growing its new “Cashies Loan” product, a revolving line of credit with no originations fees that carries an APR of 48%. The “Cashies Loan” product experiences significantly lower loss rates, and the segment is growing rapidly: in the second half of 2025 the book more than doubled from $23 Million to $58 Million. I think the market is mistakenly attributing the shrinkage of the loan book from $274.4 Million in 2024 to $230.5 Million in 2025 as a long-term trend when $42 Million out of the $43.9 Million decline is due to run-off in the payday lending and auto loan segments. With the legacy loan book down to just $57 Million (25% of total loans), I think Cash Converter’s lending operations are primed to return to single digit growth in 2026.

Not only does Cash Converters have several organic and inorganic growth opportunities, I think the market is also overlooking the possibility of a strategic takeover of Cash Converters by its 40% owner, EZ Corp International.

Cash Converters has sizeable global operations yet trades at a steep discount to both local and global peers. The stock trades at 7.5x forward earnings and 3.7x EV/EBITDA as opposed to Money3 (Australia) at 18x earnings and 11x EV/EBITDA and Latitude Financial at 10x earnings and 13x EV/EBITDA. In fact, Cash Converter’s most closely comparable peer, H&T Group (HAT LN), a UK Pawnbroker operating 285 stores, was acquired by FirstCash (FCFS US) at 13x Earnings and 5x EV/EBITDA.

Interestingly, guess who EZ Corp’s largest rival is? You guessed it, FirstCash.

As a result, Cash Converters is stand alone cheap at 7.5x forward earnings, a 6% dividend yield, notwithstanding the fact its highly aligned largest holder, EZ Corp, may one day be interested in acquiring the other 60% to compete with its archrival FirstCash. A cash or stock takeover would be highly accretive to EZ Corp (who trades at 16x forward earnings) and allow it to expand globally with minimal upfront investment.

It’s hard to predict if or when such a transaction could take place, but in the meantime I think Cash Converters will continue to execute well and that its $50 Million in annual free cash flow will provide it ample room to grow the loan book and continue buying out franchisees at < 5x EBITDA. There are still more than 160 stores in Australia and the UK, as well as 150 stores in the EU, that it can acquire. As the earnings continue to grow, the loan book is derisked, and Cash Converters returns to being a “top line growth” story, I think it will become easier for the company to secure bank financing to pursue acquisitions, creating a positive reinforcement cycle that lowers the cost of capital. Penciling in earnings of 4.5 Cents AUD in 2026 and 5.5 Cents AUD in 2027, the stock is currently trading at less than 5.5x 2027 earnings, which in my opinion, is simply too cheap to ignore. I have been adding heavily in the 0.28 to 0.31 AUD range, and I think as the story becomes clearer the stock has upside to 0.40 AUD later in the year.

Trade 5: “Leave the Mail, Take the Banking Division”

Long CTT NA (Correios de Portugal)

Conviction: Low

Sector: Logistics / Banking

Price: 6.70 EUR

Target Price: 8.00 EUR

Forward P/E: 12x

Shareholder Return Yield: 6% (Dividend: 3.0%, Share Repurchases: 3.0%)

Correios de Portugal is a 500 year old Portuguese national postal operator, but contrary to what you might immediately think the investment case has more to do with banking and very little to do with mail. While the market remains hyper-fixated on declining mail volumes, CTT’s real gems are its rapidly growing and substantially de-risked postal banking operations, and its 60%+ market share in last-mile package delivery which is poised to consistently grow from rising e-commerce adoption.

CTT is one of the fastest growing Portuguese Banks. ANACOM, the Portuguese postal regulator, requires CTT to maintain at least one full-service postal establishment in every municipality in the country, which has resulted in nearly 2,400 access points across Portugal. In 2016, CTT wisely realized it could leverage its widespread geographical footprint to provide basic banking services in regions where larger competitors were systematically closing branches, in many instances, CTT’s mail / banking outposts offer the only face-to-face financial services in miles. By having mail outposts double as local banks, CTT has been able to grow its deposit base with essentially zero customer acquisition cost and no competition. Its widespread deposit network is simply financially unfeasible for any other bank to build.

Low cost deposits have steadily grown from just 250 Million in 2016 to 4.3 Billion in 2025 and Net Interest Income has surged from 3.3 Million in 2017 to 101.9 Million in 2025.

The banking subsidiary is extremely well-capitalized and the loan-to-deposit ratio is less than 50%. Simply put, CTT’s Bank is so flush with deposits they can’t find people to lend to, and nearly 60% of deposits are parked in short-dated government bonds, providing risk free interest income. CTT’s strategic goal for 2026 is to judiciously expand lending operations to boost the banking segment’s ROE. In what is even more ironic, CTT is actually a higher for longer beneficiary given so much cash is left parked in short-dated government bonds. Talk about a plot twist for Portugal’s largest postal carrier.

There are significant cultural differences between American and Portuguese saving habits. Portuguese retirees leave a much larger portion of their net worth in cash, and frequently purchase Certificados de Aforro (Portuguese T Bills). While the certificates can be purchased online, many retirees opt to purchase these certificates in person, via CTT branches. To purchase the certificates, you need a bank account, which has enabled CTT to deeply expand its offerings in rural regions to elderly customers, opening thousands of accounts and developing a sticky deposit base that is highly unlikely to leave and extremely loyal. In response to the massive surge in deposits, CTT has expanded its auto-lending and mortgage verticals, and as lending operations mature, net income is set to surge.

Some have argued that CTT’s Banking profits are overstated because staffing and distribution (real estate) expenses are just 18 Million for a network of 2,400 deposit outputs, very low. While that is true, I think the argument is relatively flimsy anyways. CTT isn’t planning on spinning out the banking division, and its postal outposts would exist regardless of whether they offered banking services or not. CTT’s Bank is 92% owned by CTT (the other 8% is owned by Generali), so the Banking Division is simply paying the parent company a bit of rent, and whether that level of rent is higher or lower it makes no real difference to overall net income. Banking segment Net Income has steadily grown from 14 Million in 2022 to 21 Million in 2025, and now comprises 40% of CTT’s total net income. A modest increase in the loan book could boost banking income to 25 Million or higher in 2026.

I’m also attracted to CTT due to growing Portuguese e-commerce. Parcel Delivery revenues have exploded from 150 Million in 2019 to 631 Million in 2025 and are primed for further gains as online shopper penetration is just 49% in Portugal relative to 75% for the rest of the EU. CTT has recently been approved to take over DHL’s Portuguese operations and will boost its last-mile delivery market share to 70% in Portgual (Amazon has no delivery operations or fulfillment centers in Portugal, making it highly unlikely for them to develop a delivery network). CTT will also handle all of DHL’s last mile deliveries in Spain, doubling its market share from 8% to 16% in a much larger market. DHL is contributing 69 Million in cash to CTT (for use in dividends and share buybacks), and in exchange will receive 25% of CTT’s delivery segment. The transaction is highly accretive to CTT after synergies, and more importantly, ensures a dominant position in Portuguese parcel delivery.

Finally, CTT’s “achilles heel”, the mail division, is performing much better than expected because of a generous pricing mechanism approved by the Portuguese government. CTT is allowed to incorporate volume declines into its pricing, as a result, 7% annual declines in mail volume have been almost entirely offset with 7% annual postal price increases, and EBIT from the Mail division has grown over the last three years.

At the current price of 6.60 and at 12x earnings, I think the market is heavily discounting CTT’s future potential. The mail division is stable, the parcel division is likely to grow at a steady 10%+ a year, and its banking division remains an unappreciated gem. As deposits continue to roll in and lending operations develop, the division will meaningfully drive future growth.

CTT is not a monopoly, and its mail delivery pricing system is set to be renegotiated by the Portuguese Government in 2029. If the government puts a stop to 5-7% annual price increases, this would heavily impact the mail division. As with all acquisitions, it’s also possible CTT’s rosy synergies with DHL’s Portuguese operations take longer to be realized.

Nevertheless, I think CTT is within striking distance of 0.56 EUR in earnings 2026 and 0.65 EUR in 2027, placing the stock at 12x forward earnings and 10x 2027 earnings for a name that has very little competition and a long growth runway ahead of it.

As deposits continue to roll in and e-commerce activity surges, I think CTT will shed its image as a flailing mail company and be recognized for its dominant position in package delivery and its highly unique banking division. As both segments continue to grow, I think the market will realize the significant barriers to entry make them utility-like in nature, and investors will ultimately assign CTT a premium valuation. In the meantime, the company is highly attentive to the current valuation it is trading at, and has launched a 30 Million EUR buyback (3.5% of outstanding), on top of consistent dividend hikes (0.085 in 2021 to 0.12 in 2022, 0.125 in 2023, 0.17 in 2024 and 2025, and 0.19 in 2025). The 2026 dividend and repurchase program amount to roughly 6% of the current price, which isn’t bad for a “growth” name.

CTT is a low-conviction position for me right now. It is optically cheap, I like the capital returns and the growth, and I am waiting to see if the company can execute on its goals of more lending activity from the banking segment. Portuguese stocks report quarterly, so it will be easy to track progress and the company should report earnings in May. I have been adding in the 6.50 to 6.70 Range, and have left a lot of capacity to add near 6.00, which would represent 11x forward earnings. I’m not expecting much “multiple inflation” here, but I do think by 2027 CTT could still trade at 12.5x earnings, which would represent 8.00 EUR a share.

Portfolio Review

I’ve divided my Portfolio into weighted baskets. Positions aren’t equal weighted, and I’ve marked my favorites names within each basket as a “Top Pick”. The varying levels of conviction (high, medium, low) approximate my conviction and sizing within the basket. Ultimately the weights are up to you to determine.

As you’ll see below, my portfolio is disproportionately exposed to Financials, Memory, AI Infrastructure, and Japanese Equities. Regional Banks, Insurance, and Memory represent less than 10% of World Equity Market Capitalization, but more than 60% of my Portfolio. Would I recommend having disproportionate exposure to these sectors? No. I want this blog to be a place to see ideas and setups you might not usually see, when I write up Small Cap setups such as International General Insurance, CBL Properties, Chain Bridge Bancorp, and Georgia Capital, it’s to get these names on your radar. It’s entirely up to you to conduct your own due-diligence, determine if you find the thesis attractive, and whether these trades are suitable for your portfolio as well as what an appropriate weight might be. Now, let’s get into the Portfolio, and recent changes.

(Note: Western Digital was inadvertently left out of the Memory, Storage, and Tech basket at the time of publication despite being discussed below. I have since corrected the basket)

Portfolio Changes:

Additions:

MOMO US (Hello Group)

9220 JP (FB Care Services)

7089 JP (For Startups)

CTT PL (Correrios de Portugal)

Removals:

MCHB US (Mechanics Bancorp) - Total Return +22.98% - Closed April 10, 2026

MCHB, originally featured in the Dividends, Discounts, Diamonds in the Rough piece has significantly re-rated and is now trading at roughly 13x forward earnings. The bank intends to pay out a sizeable dividend in the $1.20 to $1.40 range (8 - 9% yield), which will no doubt attract the dividend investors, but I think there is very limited upside remaining on the trade. At roughly 1.9x Tangible Book Value, I think the name is certainly pricing in a large premium for their excellent management team, and that you can get significantly more value via a position in Customers Bancorp at 9x Forward Earnings and 1.15x Tangible Book.

KRNY US (Kearny Financial) - Total Return +25.80% - Closed April 10, 2026

KRNY, originally featured in the Shifting Into Rates Down, has also significantly re-rated. The stock trades at roughly 13x forward earnings, and while there is still 25% upside to Tangible Book Value of $9.93, I no longer find the setup favorable. The deposit base is extremely costly and the balance sheet has significant exposure to multifamily real estate (and a bit of NYC rent stabilized exposure). I think Kearny will perpetually trade at a discount to Tangible Book Value (absent it being acquired), and that at 13x earnings, you are no longer really getting it at deep value. Should the name trade down to $6.50, I will re-enter.

BMBL US (Bumble) - Total Return +17.07% - Closed Mar 24, 2026

Bumble is an interesting name. At 2.90 - 3.00 in February it appeared dirt cheap, and I think the company still has a lot of optionality by reducing marketing spending and trimming corporate overhead. I wanted to make a bit of room for Hello Group (MOMO) in my portfolio, and I think Bumble’s capital allocation is a bit questionable. At < 5x earnings, I think they should be redirecting 100% of Free Cash Flow into share repurchases, but the company is instead spending a lot on R&D and deleveraging. It might still work out, but at the current price ($4.03), I have no real feel on it.

Options Trading:

The implied volatility on Western Digital, and Comfort Systems is extremely high. After the recent run, in lieu of taking profits I think it makes sense to sell some covered calls on these names (assuming you own 100 shares or more).

For Western Digital, I’ve sold the January 2027 520 Strike Calls for $59 and the January 2027 540 Strike Calls for $54 on my position. The $59 for the 520’s and the $54 for the 540’s represents 16% and 15% cash upfront on my position, and still leaves 40% and 45% upside remaining. Western Digital isn’t projected to hit $20 in earnings until 2028. Even if it somehow hits that level this year, $520 and $540 would represent 26-27x earnings, a level I would be comfortable selling my shares at early next year.

Closer to the Comfort Systems (FIX) earnings report, I will collar my position. I haven’t put on the trade yet, but I will want to limit upside and downside to 200 points in either direction. Given options on Comfort Systems are skewed, the cost of a collar is usually a net credit, making it even more attractive to put on if you want to control risk.

Basket Discussions:

Memory, Storage, and Tech (~20% Weight):

SK Hynix and Google remain my highest conviction positions within this basket. I like Hynix’s blend of exposure to both DRAM / HBM, and Flash. If you apply Micron’s 5x forward multiple to Hynix’s memory business and Sandisk’s 10x forward multiple to Hynix’s flash business, the implied price per share is 1,320,000 KRW, representing 14% upside from current levels. I think Hynix’s ADR will drive significant passive inflows. Not only will the ADR make Hynix accessible to all investors, should Hynix choose to list on the Nasdaq, its 553 Billion USD market cap would rank it somewhere between the 10th and 12th largest equity on Nasdaq, making it highly eligible for the Nasdaq 100.

That may indeed be a “sell the news” event, but until then, at 5x forward earnings and little signs of the memory cycle peaking, I am happy to hold my position.

Google is my favorite member of the Magnificent 7. I believe Google’s TPU segment is underappreciated and that can allocate capital effectively. Unlike many neoclouds who are simply racing to get capacity online, Google’s deep knowledge of customer demand, Data Center construction, and internal use case provides enough data to ensure it is making judicious capital allocation decisions.

Could this be an emperor has no clothes situation where everyone (neoclouds and Google alike) spends billions and receives a minimal return on their capex? Possibly. But if anyone has a good idea of where to allocate capital, it should be Google, and I think their large 2026 Capex budget is reflection of the opportunity they see. Google trades at 28x earnings, slightly higher than the broader S&P 500 at 22x, but given the utility-like nature of their products and potential AI integration opportunities throughout their ecosystem, it’s a name I am comfortable holding at a premium to the market. I missed my chance to add more < $300, but should it trade down, I won’t miss that chance again.

AI Infrastructure (~10% Weight):

IES Holdings (IESC) remains my favorite pick within my AI Infrastructure buildout basket. I covered the name in the February 3 update, and the thesis has not changed. I think IES’s exceptional alignment (Chairman owns $5 Billion through his hedge fund Tontine Partners), history of success, and unusual strategy of vertical integration (acquisition of engine parts manufacturing and steel fabrication facilities) to become a one-stop shop differentiates IES from peers. The stock is up 30% since the February piece and is trading at mildly expensive 30x forward earnings, so I don’t necessarily think the stock is in a buying range right now. Nonetheless, I think the Q2 estimate of $3.95 is a bit low and that IES is likely to report an ever-increasing backlog, so I am maintaining my position and waiting to see Q1 earnings before making a decision on whether to add or reduce.

I think Vistance Networks is worth keeping an eye on after the $10 special dividend is distributed later this month. The company is a shell of its former self following the sale of its Connectivity and Cable Solutions segment to Amphenol. Vistance is likely to maintain profitability and grow earnings from $0.94 in 2026 to $0.98 in 2027 from its remaining Aurora Networks and Ruckus segments (campus, stadium, hospital wifi, broadband cable equipment). While Vistance is no longer an AI infrastructure name, I find the valuation compelling. The original plan was for the company to optimize its balance sheet, but in the recent 8-K detailing the special dividend, it made clear the dividend was funded solely with cash on hand, due to recent market volatility. I think the 8-K is making clear Vistance plans to eventually tap the debt market to optimize its balance sheet, which means a share repurchase program is likely going to be announced later this year. At roughly 9x post-dividend earnings, I am happy to hold Vistance.

To be upfront, I have no real feel on Comfort Systems and Powell Industries right now. While the fundamentals are growing rapidly, the valuation is reflective of this and the bar seems appropriately high for earnings. I will wait to see results before making any changes to my positions.

Banking, Insurance, and Financial Services (~40% Weight):

My top picks within this basket are Customers Bancorp (CUBI), OSB Group (OSB LN), Oppenheimer (OPY US), and International General Insurance (IGIC).

Customers Bancorp is my favorite Regional Bank position. I think the valuation (9.5x forward earnings vs 12x for the broader benchmark) is attractive, and that Customers differentiated business model (via its CUBIX vertical and specialty lending division) should eventually enable it to trade at a premium to peers. Ironically, CUBI’s success in crypto (CUBIX) and its PE / VC loan book (which has not experienced a single charge-off since inception) is penalized by the market and viewed by many as a risk. What I like about this setup is that the bar is low, and that as Customers continues to report solid results to minimal fanfare, investors will warm to the name. While it may seem like a value trap at first glance, Customers was the top performing KRE component in 2023 and 2025, and has generated a three year return of 330% vs 77% on the broader benchmark. It might take a bit of time, but the outperformance is certainly noticeable. The Q1 $1.88 consensus estimate seems within range, and I think more importantly, solid credit quality, continued deposit growth from its new banking teams, and a bit of execution on the recently announced $100 Million Repurchase Program will be highly appreciated by investors and soothe concerns over Customers Private Equity and Business Credit Loan Book (approximately $3.1 Billion). On a side note, Customers differentiates itself from peers via “Wholistic Banking”, i.e. PE and Business Credit portfolio companies use Customers as their primary bank, bringing in sizeable chunks of low-cost deposits, and giving Customers extreme visibility into credit quality since these companies maintain their primary accounts at Customers. This judicious approach is part of the reason why Customers has never had a charge-off within this segment since inception. I don’t like to add to my position at a tremendous premium to book, but I think $66 - $70 provides an attractive entry point (Q1 Tangible Book Value should be around $63.90 a share).

I covered OSB Group in the March Portfolio Review, and I continue to add the stock at a 10% discount to Tangible Book. OSB’s niche and underwriting talent in Rental Property lending has consistently generated above-average returns, and I think the acceleration of the company’s repurchase program at current prices is highly accretive to future earnings and sends a strong signal that the management team believes the stock is undervalued.

I have been steadily buying shares in the 520-540 range, and I think OSB should eventually trade at a 10% premium to Tangible Book, which would imply 630.

Oppenheimer Holdings (OPY), an Investment Bank and Wealth Manager known for municipal finance, biotechnology, and small cap equity capital markets, has been on a tear. I think the market is finally beginning to realize the value of OPY’s highly profitable and stable wealth management business, along with the right-tail optionality provided by the Capital Markets division, which drove quarterly earnings to a record $7 a share last quarter. Biotech is trading at the highest levels since 2021, equity isssuances have rebounded sharply since the Iran war.

My only real concern is that Oppenheimer’s OARs (Oppenheimer Appreciation Rights), cash-settled call options that compensate employees for upside in Oppenheimer stock, will negatively impact Q1 earnings. Currently 2.6 Million OARs are outstanding. Given the Q1 rise in OPY’s share price the company is likely to experience a negative impact of $1.70 - $1.90 on EPS.

Oppenheimer typically doesn’t report “adjusted earnings” so this may create a bit of “headline shock” when the EPS figure comes out. However, Oppenheimer tends to single out the OAR impact on Net Income if it is significant, so we should be able to see how strong the underlying business is performing. While the OAR’s will create quarter-to-quarter noise in earnings, over the long-run I think this compensation strategy (as opposed to the common US culture of zero-strike stock options and ridiculous RSU compensation) is preferable. The proof is in the pudding, and while Oppenheimer might seem like a value trap at 1.3x Book Value and 8.6x Forward Earnings, its long-term performance tells a sharply different story.

International General Insurance (IGIC), is one of my largest positions. The stock is currently trading near an ATH around 9.3x forward earnings (consensus is $3.03, my forecast is $2.80). IGIC is a consistent outperformer. Over the last 25 years its father-and-son management team have transformed it from a sleepy Middle-Eastern energy underwriter into an elite International underwriter with an industry leading metrics.

I think IGIC likely took a hit from recent events in the Middle East given their sizeable presence in reinsurance, property, and political violence lines. While this will negatively impact Q1 earnings, I believe recent events in the Middle East may catalyze a sudden wave of growth for the company.

From the commentary I’ve read, inbound inquiries across the industry for political violence (war, terrorism) coverage is up more than 800% since the war began, and political violence, marine, and marine cargo rates are up more than 300%. While it is too early to assess whether these rates hold (and what the damage from events in March is), I think IGI, with its significant capitalization, history of opportunistic underwriting, and expertise in Middle East affairs, is likely to be taking advantage of the opportunity and deploying capital where they believe the risk-to-reward is highly attractive. Many large businesses who did not carry political violence coverage are certain to be interested in adding coverage, which should provide a growth tailwind even if the situation comes to a permanent resolution.

I like to add to my position below $25. The company has historically been aggressive in the $23 - $24 a share range, making an entry point near those levels favorable as a short-term trade, as well as a long-term hold. At a 2-3x turn multiple discount to peers, and a history of excellent capital allocation, opportunistic underwriting, and highly aligned insiders, I think IGI is a quality name trading at a very palatable multiple. I am eager to see their Q1 results, and while the war will undoubtedly impact results, I am curious to see whether recent events will catalyze a massive multi-year opportunity for growth.

I have been adding to my Kaspi (KSPI) position. The stock trades at just 6.5x forward earnings with an 8%+ dividend yield. Kaspi is a Kazakh “superapp” in Kazakhstan; their payments, e-commerce marketplace, travel, lending, and grocery divisions dominate the country. The company is finally in capital return mode, armed with $45 Million in remaining repurchases and has reinstated its sizeable $1.70 a quarter dividend. I am very bullish on Kazakhstan, rising crude, gold, and uranium prices will boost the current account and provide ample support to the Kazakh Tenge. As Kaspi continues to return capital, improve its position in Turkish e-commerce, and expand its banking segment, I think it will eventually re-gain its “growth darling” status. Even a small re-rate to 8.5x earnings implies more than $100 a share. Should the name finally breakout above $85, I will add even more.

Lastly, I have been steadily adding to my Heritage Insurance (HRTG) position. The stock trades at 6x earnings, a steep discount to geographically constrained peers such as American Integrity (AII), HCI (HCI), Universal Insurance Holdings (UVE), Slide (SLDE) and American Coastal (ACIC).

Heritage maintains sizeable operations in New York and California, where conditions are increasingly favorable, and its large national presence allows it to pursue business where conditions are ripe. Unlike the peer set, which is largely tied to underwriting conditions in Florida (which should weaken considerably by the end of 2027), HRTG has the ability to pick the cream of the crop. Heritage is a heavily “under-owned” name with minimal Institutional attention. The thesis here is simple, you are getting a geographically diversified insurer at a 30% discount to geographically concentrated peers. As national growth continues and Heritage makes steady progress on its share repurchase program, I think it will eventually get some attention and trade in-line with peers (which would imply $30 a share).

Global Equities (~10% Weight):

Aside from the new positions, very little has changed in my Global Equities portfolio. I like Kazatomprom (KAP LI) at 14x earnings for Uranium exposure, and Modern Dental Group (3600 HK) for dental prosthetics exposure at a very palatable 9x earnings. SE Holdings and Incubations (9478 JP), a sleepy Japanese publisher with a portfolio of cash and equities larger than its market cap, remains one of my favorite ways to get exposure to Japan at a discount, and I have also added in HSI and Topix futures at 3% weight each to get index exposure.

I believe that China has witnessed the positive impact of the Capital Allocation reforms conducted by Japan and Korea, and is eager to replicate the same for itself. With the HSI trading at 11x earnings, the Topix at 17x, and the SPX around 21x, I think it is worth considering Hong Kong and Japan exposure either via index futures (MHI, MNTPX), or ETFs (EWH, EWJ). I will have more updates on the Global Equities portfolio as Q1 results roll in.

General Commentary and Conclusion

The market’s recent comeback has been remarkable. I think record amounts of cash were left on the sidelines which may lead to a slow drift higher as people begrudgingly buy back in (my cash balance has dropped from 20% to 10% after accounting for the new holdings, and positions in HSI and Topix futures). On top of cash coming off the sidelines, another question I think of is will Trump want to jawbone markets lower prior to the midterms? Knowing how attentive he is to markets, probably not.

I’m hopeful we can have a slow grind up towards the fall, similar to 2025, but my approach remains the same regardless: stay disciplined, hold your best ideas at a comfortable weight (< 10%), and don’t be forced into pressured decisions you’ll regret in either direction. The investors who get hurt most in volatile markets are those who either panic-sell the lows, or those who leverage up after proclaiming a bottom just a week into a drawdown. 90% of the Portfolio is up significantly since February, after a nauseating 15% drop. Had you taken a 6 week vacation, you would’ve gotten some time in the sun, avoided spiking your blood pressure, and opened up your laptop to discovers several special dividends (IGIC, CBL) and fresh highs.

Even after the recent run, valuations in the Portfolio are reasonable. More than 60% have an active share repurchase program, and 44 out of 45 names are profitable (Entravision is not profitable, but it’s a growth story). I’m hopeful that as inflecting fundamentals and shareholder friendly capital allocation programs continue, the good times will roll.

As always, will be covering trade exits and any time sensitive updates in the chat, should they arise.
